title: Class 4
text:
This class has three distinct parts: (1) what happens to OLS as the sample grows; (2) how to include qualitative information in regressions; and (3) what happens when the error variance is not constant. The common question is: when can we trust an estimated coefficient and the inference attached to it?




An estimator is consistent if it converges in probability to the true population parameter as the sample size increases:
\[
\operatorname{plim}_{n\to\infty}\hat\beta_j=\beta_j.
\]
Intuitively, as we collect more observations, the probability that our estimate is far from the true value tends to zero. The sampling-distribution diagram on lecture slide 4 shows distributions becoming increasingly concentrated around the true coefficient.
Consistency is not the same as unbiasedness. Unbiasedness means \(E(\hat\beta_j)=\beta_j\) for a given sample size; consistency concerns what happens as \(n\to\infty\). An estimator can be biased in finite samples but consistent. Conversely, unbiasedness alone does not guarantee consistency.
For the multiple regression model
\[
y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{1i}+\cdots+\beta_kx_{ki}+u_i,
\]
the lecture states that OLS is consistent under MLR.1–MLR.4:







Assumption
Meaning




MLR.1: linear in parameters
The regression is linear in the unknown \(\beta\) coefficients.


MLR.2: random sampling
Observations are independently drawn from the population.


MLR.3: no perfect collinearity
No regressor is an exact linear combination of the others; sufficient variation exists.


MLR.4: zero conditional mean
\(E(u\mid x_1,\ldots,x_k)=0\).



Why MLR.4 matters: it rules out systematic links between the regressors and unobserved determinants of \(y\). Under suitable regularity conditions, a weaker requirement—\(E(u)=0\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(x_j,u)=0\) for each regressor—is sufficient for consistency. This is not generally sufficient for finite-sample unbiasedness.



If a regressor is correlated with the error term, increasing the sample size does not necessarily fix the problem. In simple regression,
\[
\operatorname{plim}\hat\beta_1
=\beta_1+\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(x,u)}{\operatorname{Var}(x)}.
\]
The extra term is the asymptotic bias (the difference between the probability limit and the true coefficient). Positive covariance produces upward asymptotic bias; negative covariance produces downward asymptotic bias.
Example: suppose we regress wages on education but omit ability. If ability raises wages and is positively correlated with education, the estimated education coefficient can remain too high even with an enormous sample. More observations do not cure endogeneity.






Important



Multiple-regression nuance: correlation between one regressor and the error threatens consistency, but does not logically imply that every OLS coefficient must be inconsistent. The direction and size of each coefficient’s asymptotic bias depend on the entire regressor covariance structure.





Class 3 used a normality assumption (MLR.6) to justify exact finite-sample \(t\) and \(F\) distributions. Many outcomes are not conditionally normal. The lecture’s slide 9 gives the participation rate in a 401(k) pension plan: it lies between 0 and 100, and many observations equal 100. Such an outcome cannot have an unrestricted normal conditional distribution.
Fortunately, the central limit theorem often gives a large-sample approximation:
\[
\frac{\hat\beta_j-\beta_j}{\operatorname{se}(\hat\beta_j)}
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}N(0,1).
\]
Here \(\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}\) means converges in distribution. Under the lecture’s MLR.1–MLR.5 and the usual regularity conditions, conventional OLS standard errors support this result even without MLR.6. MLR.5 is homoskedasticity, or constant conditional error variance.
This makes familiar procedures approximately valid in sufficiently large samples:

Two-sided test: reject \(H_0:\beta_j=b\) at approximately 5% if \(|t|>1.96\), where \(t=(\hat\beta_j-b)/\operatorname{se}(\hat\beta_j)\).
Approximate 95% confidence interval: \(\hat\beta_j\pm1.96\operatorname{se}(\hat\beta_j)\).
Joint tests: use large-sample approximations for \(F\)-type statistics.

There is no universal minimum sample size that guarantees a good normal approximation. Strong skewness, outliers, dependence and weak identifying variation can make it poor.






Note



Do not confuse two conditions. Non-normality of errors is often manageable with large-sample inference. Heteroskedasticity is a separate issue: it makes conventional standard errors unreliable even in large samples, so robust standard errors may be needed (Part III).





Under MLR.1–MLR.5, OLS is BLUE (best linear unbiased estimator) in finite samples. It also has an asymptotic efficiency property within an appropriate class of regular estimators using the same moment information: it achieves the smallest asymptotic variance under the stated conditions.
Interpret carefully: “best” does not mean best among every imaginable estimator in every model. The result relies on the assumptions, particularly homoskedasticity; under heteroskedasticity, alternative weighting methods may be more efficient.






A dummy variable (indicator) records whether an observation belongs to a category:
\[
female_i=\begin{cases}1,&\text{category coded as female},\\0,&\text{reference category coded as male}.\end{cases}
\]
The lecture uses this binary coding as an illustration. The key is to define what 1 and 0 mean; coding conventions are not intrinsic properties of people.
Consider the wage model on slides 18–20:
\[
wage_i=\beta_0+\beta_1female_i+\beta_2educ_i+u_i.
\]
Holding education fixed:

Reference group (\(female=0\)): \(E(wage\mid female=0,educ)=\beta_0+\beta_2educ\).
Other group (\(female=1\)): \(E(wage\mid female=1,educ)=\beta_0+\beta_1+\beta_2educ\).
Conditional difference: \(\beta_1\).

The two regression lines have different intercepts but the same slope (as illustrated on slide 19). If \(\beta_1=-2\), the model predicts wages that are £2 per hour lower for the coded female group at the same education level. This is a conditional association, not automatically a causal effect.
Changing the reference group changes the sign of the dummy coefficient but not the fitted predictions. With an intercept, including both complementary indicators (\(female\) and \(male\)) creates perfect multicollinearity, since \(female+male=1\). Alternatively, omit the intercept and include both indicators.



The lecture reports the following estimated regression for 105 Michigan manufacturing firms:
\[
\widehat{hrsemp}=46.67+26.25\,grant-0.98\log(sales)-6.07\log(employ),
\]
where \(hrsemp\) is training hours per employee and \(grant=1\) if the firm received a training grant in 1988. The standard error of the grant coefficient is 5.59, so its \(t\) statistic is approximately \(26.25/5.59=4.70\).
Interpretation: controlling for sales and employment, grant recipients have 26.25 more training hours per employee on average than non-recipients in the fitted model. This is statistically significant; it is not automatically the causal effect of receiving a grant because selection into the grant programme may matter.



With \(g\) mutually exclusive, exhaustive categories, use \(g-1\) indicators plus an intercept. The omitted category is the reference group. Every included dummy coefficient compares its category with that group, holding other regressors fixed.
The lecture combines two binary characteristics—\(female\) and \(married\)—into four groups:
\[
\begin{aligned}
marrmale&=married(1-female),\\
marrfem&=married\cdot female,\\
singmale&=(1-married)(1-female),\\
singfem&=(1-married)female.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking single men as the reference group gives
\[
\log(wage)=\beta_0+\delta_1marrmale+\delta_2marrfem+\delta_3singfem+\text{controls}+u.
\]
The lecture’s slide 24 reports \(\hat\delta_1=0.213\), \(\hat\delta_2=-0.198\) and \(\hat\delta_3=-0.110\), controlling for education, experience and tenure (including squared terms). For a log-wage dependent variable:

A dummy coefficient \(\delta\) gives an approximate \(100\delta\%\) wage difference.
The exact percentage difference is \(100(e^\delta-1)\%\).
Thus \(0.213\) means approximately 21.3%, or exactly 23.7%, higher predicted wages relative to the reference group, holding controls fixed.

Comparing two non-reference groups requires subtracting coefficients. For example, the fitted log-wage difference between married and single women is \(-0.198-(-0.110)=-0.088\). Testing whether it is zero requires the standard error of that difference, including the covariance between the two estimated coefficients.
Ordinal categories (for example, a 1–5 rating) can be entered as a single numerical regressor, imposing a constant increment per step, or as \(g-1\) indicators, allowing flexible category differences. The flexible model uses more parameters and may be less precise.






Important



Interpretation warning (slide 24): the observed wage differences do not establish that marriage itself changes wages. Selection, omitted characteristics and other explanations remain possible.





A dummy alone changes the intercept. To allow different slopes, interact the dummy with a quantitative regressor (slides 27–28):
\[
\log(wage)=\beta_0+\beta_1female+\beta_2educ+\beta_3(female\cdot educ)+u.
\]








Group
Conditional regression line
Return to an extra year of education




\(female=0\)
\(\beta_0+\beta_2educ\)
\(\beta_2\)


\(female=1\)
\((\beta_0+\beta_1)+(\beta_2+\beta_3)educ\)
\(\beta_2+\beta_3\)



Thus \(\beta_3\) is the difference in education slopes. Test \(H_0:\beta_3=0\) to test equal slopes. The group difference at education level \(e\) is \(\beta_1+\beta_3e\); \(\beta_1\) alone is the difference at \(educ=0\), which may be outside the relevant data range. For easier interpretation, education can be centred around a meaningful value.



The Chow test is a joint test of whether regression coefficients differ across two groups (slides 29–32). In the lecture’s college-GPA example, the outcome is cumulative GPA and the regressors are SAT score, high-school rank percentile and total college-course hours.
Let \(D=female\). A fully interacted model allows a different intercept and different slopes:
\[
\begin{aligned}
cumgpa={}&\beta_0+\beta_1sat+\beta_2hsperc+\beta_3tothrs\\
&+\delta_0D+\delta_1(D\cdot sat)+\delta_2(D\cdot hsperc)
+\delta_3(D\cdot tothrs)+u.
\end{aligned}
\]
There are two different questions:

Same entire regression function? \(H_0:\delta_0=\delta_1=\delta_2=\delta_3=0\) (four restrictions).
Same slopes, but possibly different intercepts? \(H_0:\delta_1=\delta_2=\delta_3=0\) (three restrictions).

The lecture’s slide 32 reports that the first test rejects at the 1% level, whereas the slope-only test has \(p=0.205\) and does not reject at conventional levels. These are not contradictory: the full test also examines the intercept difference. Failure to reject equal slopes does not prove that slopes are identical.






Homoskedasticity (MLR.5):
\[
\operatorname{Var}(u_i\mid X_i)=\sigma^2.
\]
Heteroskedasticity:
\[
\operatorname{Var}(u_i\mid X_i)=\sigma_i^2,
\]
where \(\sigma_i^2\) varies with the regressors or across observations. For example, high-income households may have much more variable spending than low-income households.
Under exogeneity and the other relevant conditions:

OLS coefficients can remain unbiased and consistent.
Fitted values and the algebraic definition of \(R^2\) are unchanged.
OLS is not generally BLUE when error variances differ.
Conventional homoskedasticity-based standard errors are generally incorrect, so the associated conventional \(t\) and \(F\) reference distributions are not justified.

The problem is inference, not necessarily the estimated coefficient.



The lecture’s slides 36–38 introduce the Huber–White (sandwich) estimator. It replaces the common error variance assumption with squared OLS residuals that can differ across observations.
The resulting robust standard error is the square root of a robust estimated coefficient variance. A robust test statistic is
\[
t_{robust}=\frac{\hat\beta_j-b}{\operatorname{se}_{robust}(\hat\beta_j)}.
\]
It is used with a large-sample normal approximation (or an appropriate large-sample reference distribution). Joint restrictions can be tested with a heteroskedasticity-robust Wald test, often reported in \(F\) form.






Warning



Robust standard errors do not fix omitted-variable bias, reverse causality, measurement error, dependence between observations or a misspecified conditional mean. They correct the estimated uncertainty for heteroskedasticity under suitable sampling and moment conditions; they do not change the OLS point estimates.













Question
Key answer




Does more data make OLS correct?
Only if the consistency conditions hold; endogeneity may cause persistent asymptotic bias.


Must errors be normal?
Not for OLS consistency; sufficiently large samples can justify approximate inference.


What does a dummy coefficient mean?
A difference relative to the omitted reference category, holding other variables fixed.


Why omit one of \(g\) category dummies?
To avoid perfect collinearity with the intercept.


What does a dummy–continuous interaction do?
Allows slopes to differ between groups.


What does a Chow test assess?
Joint equality of regression functions or, with modified restrictions, equality of slopes.


What if errors are heteroskedastic?
OLS may remain consistent, but conventional standard errors can fail; use appropriate robust inference.

title: Class 4
text:
Mathematical Derivations

1. Consistency of the simple-regression slope
Start from the population model \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+u_i\). The OLS slope is
\[
\hat\beta_1=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2}.
\]
Substitute the population model, using \(\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat\beta_1
&=\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+u_i)}{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2}\\
&=\beta_1+\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)u_i}{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Divide numerator and denominator by \(n\):
\[
\hat\beta_1=\beta_1+
\frac{n^{-1}\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)u_i}{n^{-1}\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2}.
\]
By the law of large numbers, assuming finite relevant moments and \(\operatorname{Var}(x)>0\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
n^{-1}\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)u_i&\overset{p}{\longrightarrow}\operatorname{Cov}(x,u),\\
n^{-1}\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2&\overset{p}{\longrightarrow}\operatorname{Var}(x).
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, by the continuous mapping theorem,
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{plim}\hat\beta_1=\beta_1+
\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(x,u)}{\operatorname{Var}(x)}}.
\]
If \(\operatorname{Cov}(x,u)=0\), then \(\operatorname{plim}\hat\beta_1=\beta_1\). If not, the ratio is the asymptotic bias.


2. Multiple-regression consistency in matrix form
Write \(y=X\beta+u\), where \(X\) includes an intercept and has full column rank. Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat\beta&=(X'X)^{-1}X'y\\
&=\beta+(X'X)^{-1}X'u\\
&=\beta+\left(\frac{X'X}{n}\right)^{-1}\frac{X'u}{n}.
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(n^{-1}X'X\overset{p}{\to}Q\) with \(Q\) nonsingular and \(n^{-1}X'u\overset{p}{\to}0\), then
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{plim}\hat\beta=\beta}.
\]
This makes the central requirement explicit: sample regressor–error products must average towards zero. Zero conditional mean is sufficient, but stronger than necessary for this probability-limit argument.


3. Deriving asymptotic normality
From the same identity,
\[
\sqrt n(\hat\beta-\beta)
=\left(\frac{X'X}{n}\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{X'u}{\sqrt n}\right).
\]
Under independent sampling, exogeneity and appropriate finite-moment conditions, the multivariate central limit theorem gives
\[
\frac{X'u}{\sqrt n}\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}N(0,\Omega),
\qquad \Omega=E[X_iX_i'u_i^2].
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\sqrt n(\hat\beta-\beta)\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N(0,Q^{-1}\Omega Q^{-1})}.
\]
Under homoskedasticity, \(\Omega=\sigma^2Q\), so the asymptotic covariance simplifies to \(\sigma^2Q^{-1}\). With a consistent standard error estimate, the standardised coefficient converges to \(N(0,1)\) by Slutsky’s theorem. This is the mathematical basis for the approximate tests described in Part I.


4. Reversing a binary reference group
Start from \(y=\beta_0+\beta_1female+\beta_2educ+u\). Since \(male=1-female\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
y&=\beta_0+\beta_1(1-male)+\beta_2educ+u\\
&=(\beta_0+\beta_1)-\beta_1male+\beta_2educ+u.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence, if the new model is \(y=\alpha_0+\alpha_1male+\alpha_2educ+u\),
\[
\boxed{\alpha_0=\beta_0+\beta_1,\qquad\alpha_1=-\beta_1,\qquad\alpha_2=\beta_2}.
\]
The fitted regression function is unchanged: only the baseline and sign convention differ.


5. Deriving group-specific intercepts and slopes
For \(D\in\{0,1\}\), consider
\[
E(y\mid D,x)=\beta_0+\beta_1D+\beta_2x+\beta_3Dx.
\]
Set \(D=0\) and \(D=1\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
E(y\mid D=0,x)&=\beta_0+\beta_2x,\\
E(y\mid D=1,x)&=(\beta_0+\beta_1)+(\beta_2+\beta_3)x.
\end{aligned}
\]
Subtract the two conditional means:
\[
\boxed{E(y\mid D=1,x)-E(y\mid D=0,x)=\beta_1+\beta_3x}.
\]
Therefore \(\beta_1\) is the difference at \(x=0\) and \(\beta_3\) is the difference in slopes. To test a group difference at a particular \(x=x_0\), test \(H_0:\beta_1+x_0\beta_3=0\); its variance is
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1+x_0\hat\beta_3)=
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1)+x_0^2\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_3)
+2x_0\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\beta_1,\hat\beta_3).
\]


6. Deriving the Chow-test statistic
Suppose there are \(k\) slopes plus one intercept in each group’s regression. The unrestricted model estimates a separate regression for each group, using \(2(k+1)\) parameters in total. Its residual sum of squares is
\[
SSR_U=SSR_1+SSR_2.
\]
To test equality of all coefficients, the restricted model pools both groups and estimates \(k+1\) parameters. Denote its residual sum of squares by \(SSR_R=SSR_P\). There are \(q=k+1\) restrictions, so
\[
\boxed{F=\frac{[SSR_P-(SSR_1+SSR_2)]/(k+1)}{(SSR_1+SSR_2)/[n-2(k+1)]}}.
\]
Under the classical homoskedastic normal-error assumptions and the null,
\[
F\sim F_{k+1,\,n-2(k+1)}.
\]
Slope equality only: keep a group dummy in the restricted pooled regression (allowing distinct intercepts), but omit the \(k\) slope interactions. Now \(q=k\), while the unrestricted residual degrees of freedom remain \(n-2(k+1)\):
\[
\boxed{F_{slopes}=\frac{(SSR_{R,slopes}-SSR_U)/k}{SSR_U/[n-2(k+1)]}}.
\]
Example from slide 32: with \(k=3\) and \(n=366\), the unrestricted residual degrees of freedom are \(366-2(4)=358\). The lecture reports \(R_U^2\approx0.406\) and \(R_R^2\approx0.352\) for the full-equality test. Because both models use the same dependent variable and sample,
\[
F=\frac{(R_U^2-R_R^2)/(k+1)}{(1-R_U^2)/[n-2(k+1)]}
\approx\frac{(0.406-0.352)/4}{(1-0.406)/358}
\approx8.14.
\]
(The reported \(R^2\) values are rounded, so the result is approximate.) The lecture reports a very small \(p\)-value for this joint test. If heteroskedasticity is present, this classical SSR-based \(F\) reference distribution is not generally valid; use a robust Wald test.


7. Why heteroskedasticity changes the slope variance
In simple regression, conditional on the observed \(x_i\) values,
\[
\hat\beta_1-\beta_1=\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)u_i}{SST_x},
\qquad SST_x=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2.
\]
If errors are conditionally uncorrelated across observations and \(\operatorname{Var}(u_i\mid X)=\sigma_i^2\), then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1\mid X)
&=\operatorname{Var}\left(\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)u_i}{SST_x}\,\middle|\,X\right)\\
&=\boxed{\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2\sigma_i^2}{SST_x^2}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
With homoskedasticity, \(\sigma_i^2=\sigma^2\) for every \(i\), giving
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1\mid X)=\frac{\sigma^2}{SST_x}.
\]
The second expression is not generally correct when \(\sigma_i^2\) varies.


8. Deriving the Huber–White robust variance estimator
Replace each unknown \(\sigma_i^2\) with the corresponding squared OLS residual \(\hat u_i^2\):
\[
\boxed{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}_{HC0}(\hat\beta_1)=
\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2\hat u_i^2}{SST_x^2}}.
\]
For multiple regression, let \(\hat r_{ij}\) be the residual from regressing regressor \(x_j\) on all the other regressors, including the intercept, and let \(SSR_j=\sum_i\hat r_{ij}^2\). The lecture’s coefficient-specific formula is
\[
\boxed{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}_{HC0}(\hat\beta_j)=
\frac{\sum_i\hat r_{ij}^{\,2}\hat u_i^{\,2}}{SSR_j^2}}.
\]
Its square root is the heteroskedasticity-robust standard error. In matrix notation, the corresponding HC0 covariance estimator is
\[
\boxed{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}_{HC0}(\hat\beta)=
(X'X)^{-1}X'\operatorname{diag}(\hat u_1^2,\ldots,\hat u_n^2)X(X'X)^{-1}}.
\]
The lecture gives the basic HC0 formula. Other implementations may use small-sample or leverage corrections (HC1, HC2, HC3), so reported robust standard errors need not be numerically identical across software settings.
For \(q\) joint linear restrictions \(H_0:R\beta=r\), a heteroskedasticity-robust Wald statistic is
\[
W=(R\hat\beta-r)'[R\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}_{robust}(\hat\beta)R']^{-1}(R\hat\beta-r).
\]
Under the null and appropriate large-sample conditions, \(W\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}\chi_q^2\). Software may report \(W/q\) in an \(F\)-style format, but its finite-sample reference distribution is not generally the classical Chow \(F\) distribution.

title: Class 7
text:
Ordinary least squares (OLS) estimates the effect of \(x\) on \(y\) consistently only when the explanatory variable is exogenous: it is uncorrelated with the regression error. An endogenous explanatory variable is correlated with that error. Omitted variables, reverse causality and measurement error can produce endogeneity.
Consider the return to education:
\[
\log(wage_i)=\beta_0+\beta_1 educ_i+\beta_2 abil_i+e_i.
\]
Ability is not observed. If we omit it, the estimated equation becomes
\[
\log(wage_i)=\beta_0+\beta_1 educ_i+u_i,
\qquad u_i=\beta_2 abil_i+e_i.
\]
If education and ability are correlated, then \(\operatorname{Cov}(educ_i,u_i)\ne0\) (assuming the other error component does not offset this relationship). OLS confuses the effect of education with the effect of ability.
Panel-data fixed effects and first differences can remove time-invariant unobserved characteristics, but cannot automatically remove time-varying confounders or identify the effects of time-invariant regressors. Instrumental variables (IV) offer another approach. This lecture considers IV primarily with cross-sectional random samples.



For the structural equation
\[
y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+u_i,
\]
an instrument \(z_i\) must satisfy two distinct conditions:

Exogeneity: \(\operatorname{Cov}(z_i,u_i)=0\). The instrument must not be related to unobserved determinants of \(y\).
Relevance: \(\operatorname{Cov}(z_i,x_i)\ne0\). The instrument must predict the endogenous regressor.

For a causal interpretation, we also need a credible exclusion restriction: \(z\) affects \(y\) through \(x\), not through an additional direct channel. This is part of the substantive argument for instrument validity; correlation alone cannot establish it.
Intuition: IV isolates the part of \(x\) that moves with \(z\) rather than with the problematic error \(u\). In a diagram, the intended channel is \(z\rightarrow x\rightarrow y\), while unobserved influences \(u\) affect both \(x\) and \(y\). There must be no unblocked path from \(z\) to \(y\) other than through \(x\).
Example: education and wages. IQ scores may predict education but also reflect ability, so exogeneity is doubtful. A parent’s education may predict a child’s education but also correlate with family advantages affecting wages. Number of siblings may predict schooling, but family circumstances may invalidate the exclusion restriction. These are candidate instruments, not automatically valid instruments.
We can investigate relevance with a first-stage regression of \(x\) on \(z\). We cannot establish exogeneity merely by running that regression: economic reasoning and institutional knowledge are essential.



With one endogenous regressor and one instrument,
\[
\boxed{\hat\beta_{1,IV}=\frac{\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}(z,y)}{\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}(z,x)}}.
\]
Interpretation: how strongly the instrument changes the outcome, divided by how strongly it changes the explanatory variable. For example, if an instrument raises schooling by \(0.5\) years and log wages by \(0.03\), the IV slope is \(0.03/0.5=0.06\): approximately a 6% wage increase per extra year of schooling, provided the instrument is valid.
If \(x\) is exogenous and we choose \(z=x\), this formula reduces to OLS. IV is consistent under the stated conditions, but may be substantially biased in small samples.



IV generally sacrifices precision to address endogeneity. Under homoskedasticity, its approximate slope variance is
\[
\operatorname{Avar}(\hat\beta_{1,IV})
=\frac{\sigma_u^2}{n\sigma_x^2\rho_{xz}^2}.
\]
Here \(\rho_{xz}^2\) is the squared correlation between the instrument and the endogenous regressor. When it is small, the IV estimate is imprecise. Heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors are available.
A weak instrument predicts \(x\) only weakly. Weak instruments can cause substantial finite-sample bias and make conventional confidence intervals and hypothesis tests unreliable, even in large samples. The lecture mentions the familiar first-stage \(F>10\) rule of thumb. This is a screening heuristic, not a guarantee of strong identification or reliable inference, especially with multiple instruments or heteroskedasticity.
The lecture cites quarter of birth as an instrument for schooling (Angrist and Krueger, 1991), and subsequent concerns about its weakness (Bound, Jaeger and Baker, 1995).
Do not judge IV by its \(R^2\). Unlike OLS, IV does not choose coefficients to minimise squared residuals, so its conventional \(R^2=1-SSR/SST\) may be lower than OLS’s or even negative. The purpose is credible estimation of a structural effect, not maximising fit.

\[

Suppose the structural model contains one endogenous regressor \(y_2\), one included exogenous control \(z_1\), and two excluded instruments \(z_2,z_3\):
\[
y_1=\beta_0+\beta_1y_2+\beta_2z_1+u_1.
\]
Using only one instrument would discard information in the other. Two-stage least squares (2SLS) combines the instruments:
Stage 1 — predict the endogenous variable using all exogenous variables:
\[
y_2=\pi_0+\pi_1z_1+\pi_2z_2+\pi_3z_3+v_2.
\]
Obtain the fitted values \(\hat y_2\). The first-stage joint relevance question is whether \(\pi_2=\pi_3=0\); a joint \(F\) test is informative, subject to the weak-instrument caveat.
Stage 2 — estimate the structural relationship using predicted \(y_2\):
\[

\]
The fitted values use only variation explained by the instruments and included exogenous controls. This two-regression procedure gives the 2SLS point estimates.






WarningDo not use ordinary second-stage OLS standard errors



Although the two regressions reproduce the 2SLS coefficients, ordinary OLS standard errors from the second regression are generally incorrect because \(\hat y_2\) is estimated. Use a proper IV/2SLS estimator with appropriate standard errors (robust or clustered where required).


With one endogenous regressor, identification requires at least one relevant excluded instrument; with several endogenous regressors, there must be enough instruments and sufficient independent predictive variation (the rank condition). More instruments do not compensate for invalid instruments.
Lecture example: Using both parents’ education as instruments for schooling, the married-working-women example reports a first-stage joint \(F=55.4\) and a 2SLS education coefficient of 0.061 (SE 0.031) in a specification that also controls for experience and its square. This is approximately a 6.1% return, with greater precision than the single-instrument estimate reported earlier, though the specifications differ.



The lecture examines whether higher average hourly earnings cause drivers to work more hours on Uber. The model is
\[
\log(h_{it})=\beta_0+\beta_1\log(w_{it})+X_{it}'\gamma+u_{it},
\]
where \(h_{it}\) is weekly Uber hours and \(w_{it}\) is average hourly earnings, after Uber fees but before vehicle expenses. The coefficient \(\beta_1\) is an elasticity: a 1% increase in hourly earnings corresponds to approximately a \(\beta_1\)% change in Uber hours.
Why not OLS? Drivers choose when and where to work, while demand conditions affect earnings. Working additional less-profitable hours may itself reduce average hourly earnings: the direction of causation is not simply earnings \(\rightarrow\) hours.
Instrument: In Boston in 2016, randomly selected drivers were offered a week without Uber’s usual commission. Define \(Z_{it}=1\) if offered fee-free driving. Around 64% opted in. The offer—not actual take-up—is the instrument. Random assignment supports independence within assignment groups, but exclusion still requires that the offer affects hours only through hourly earnings.

First stage: the offer raises log hourly earnings by 0.20 (SE 0.01).
OLS elasticity: 0.21 (SE 0.06).
IV/2SLS elasticity: 1.16 (SE 0.12).

The IV estimate implies approximately 1.16% more Uber hours for a 1% increase in hourly earnings in the setting studied. It concerns a temporary earnings change; it does not automatically imply the same response to permanent wage changes. Drivers may also reallocate hours from other platforms or jobs, so increased Uber hours need not mean increased total working hours.
The lecture reports 1,176 drivers and 2,214 observations with positive hours; standard errors are clustered by driver. The study is Angrist, Caldwell and Hall (2021), Uber versus Taxi: A Driver’s Eye View.






NoteThe central IV checklist



Before interpreting any IV estimate, ask: (1) What makes \(x\) endogenous? (2) What is the instrument? (3) Why should it predict \(x\) conditional on controls? (4) Why should it have no other route to \(y\)? (5) Is the first stage strong enough? (6) Are the standard errors appropriate? (7) Which population and type of variation does the estimate describe?

text:
Mathematical Derivations

1. Omitted-variable bias (slides 4–5)
Suppose the true model is
\[
y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{1i}+\beta_2x_{2i}+e_i,
\qquad E(e_i\mid x_{1i},x_{2i})=0.
\]
If we regress \(y\) only on \(x_1\), the population regression slope is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\tilde\beta_1
&=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(x_1,y)}{\operatorname{Var}(x_1)}\\
&=\beta_1+\beta_2\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(x_1,x_2)}{\operatorname{Var}(x_1)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Writing \(\delta_1=\operatorname{Cov}(x_1,x_2)/\operatorname{Var}(x_1)\), we obtain
\[
\boxed{\tilde\beta_1-\beta_1=\beta_2\delta_1.}
\]
Sign: omitted-variable bias is positive when the omitted factor raises \(y\) (\(\beta_2>0\)) and is positively associated with \(x_1\) (\(\delta_1>0\)). If either factor is zero, this particular bias disappears.


2. Deriving the simple IV estimator (slides 6, 10–11)
Start with \(y=\beta_0+\beta_1x+u\) and assume \(\operatorname{Cov}(z,u)=0\). Taking covariance with \(z\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Cov}(z,y)
&=\operatorname{Cov}(z,\beta_0+\beta_1x+u)\\
&=\beta_1\operatorname{Cov}(z,x)+\operatorname{Cov}(z,u)\\
&=\beta_1\operatorname{Cov}(z,x).
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(\operatorname{Cov}(z,x)\ne0\), divide to identify the coefficient:
\[
\boxed{\beta_1=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(z,y)}{\operatorname{Cov}(z,x)}}.
\]
Replace population covariances by sample analogues:
\[
\boxed{\hat\beta_{1,IV}=
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(z_i-\bar z)(y_i-\bar y)}
{\sum_{i=1}^n(z_i-\bar z)(x_i-\bar x)}};
\qquad
\hat\beta_{0,IV}=\bar y-\hat\beta_{1,IV}\bar x.
\]
The denominator explains why weak relevance is dangerous: if \(z\) hardly varies with \(x\), small sampling fluctuations can create large changes in the ratio.


3. The first-stage slope and identification (slides 8, 18–19)
The population linear projection of \(x\) on \(z\) is
\[
x=\pi_0+\pi_1z+v,
\qquad \pi_1=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(z,x)}{\operatorname{Var}(z)}.
\]
Thus \(\pi_1\ne0\) is equivalent to instrument relevance, provided \(\operatorname{Var}(z)>0\). In a simple first stage, testing \(H_0:\pi_1=0\) is a direct test of zero linear association; rejecting it does not prove the instrument is sufficiently strong for reliable IV inference.


4. Large-sample variance and the weak-instrument penalty (slides 12–14)
With independent observations, instrument exogeneity, finite moments and homoskedasticity \(E(u^2\mid z)=\sigma_u^2\),
\[
\operatorname{Avar}(\hat\beta_{1,IV})
=\frac{\sigma_u^2\operatorname{Var}(z)}{n\operatorname{Cov}(z,x)^2}.
\]
Since \(\operatorname{Cov}(z,x)=\rho_{xz}\sigma_x\sigma_z\),
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Avar}(\hat\beta_{1,IV})
=\frac{\sigma_u^2}{n\sigma_x^2\rho_{xz}^2}}.
\]
Using \(SST_x=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2\) and the first-stage \(R^2=\hat\rho_{xz}^2\),
\[
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta_{1,IV})
\approx\frac{\hat\sigma_u^2}{SST_xR_{x,z}^2},
\qquad
\hat\sigma_u^2=\frac{\sum_i\hat u_i^2}{n-2},
\quad \hat u_i=y_i-\hat\beta_{0,IV}-\hat\beta_{1,IV}x_i.
\]
The estimated standard error is the square root of this variance. Relative to the analogous OLS variance formula under exogeneity, \(1/R_{x,z}^2\) is the IV variance inflation factor. Important: when OLS is endogenous, its usual standard error describes uncertainty around an inconsistent estimator; a smaller OLS standard error does not make OLS preferable.


5. IV in multiple regression: moment conditions (slides 22–24)
Let
\[
y_{1i}=\beta_0+\beta_1y_{2i}+\beta_2z_{1i}+u_{1i},
\]
where \(z_1\) is an exogenous control and \(z_2\) is an excluded instrument. Assume
\[
E(u_1)=0,\qquad E(z_1u_1)=0,\qquad E(z_2u_1)=0.
\]
Define \(\hat u_{1i}=y_{1i}-\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1y_{2i}-\hat\beta_2z_{1i}\). The sample moment equations are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_i\hat u_{1i}&=0,\\
\sum_i z_{1i}\hat u_{1i}&=0,\\
\sum_i z_{2i}\hat u_{1i}&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
These give three equations for three coefficients, provided the instruments supply sufficient independent variation. Notice that every residual contains \(\hat\beta_2z_{1i}\): the included control must not accidentally be replaced by \(z_2\).
The first-stage equation \(y_2=\pi_0+\pi_1z_1+\pi_2z_2+v_2\) identifies the relevance requirement \(\pi_2\ne0\) conditional on \(z_1\).


6. Reduced form and the IV ratio with controls (slide 32)
Substitute the first stage into the structural equation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_1&=\beta_0+\beta_1(\pi_0+\pi_1z_1+\pi_2z_2+v_2)+\beta_2z_1+u_1\\
&=(\beta_0+\beta_1\pi_0)+(\beta_2+\beta_1\pi_1)z_1
+\beta_1\pi_2z_2+(u_1+\beta_1v_2).
\end{aligned}
\]
If the reduced form for \(y_1\) is \(y_1=\alpha_0+\alpha_1z_1+\alpha_2z_2+e\), then \(\alpha_2=\beta_1\pi_2\) and therefore
\[
\boxed{\beta_1=\frac{\alpha_2}{\pi_2}\quad\text{if }\pi_2\ne0.}
\]
This is the conditional counterpart of the simple covariance-ratio estimator: the instrument’s effect on the outcome divided by its effect on the endogenous regressor, holding the control fixed.


7. Deriving 2SLS as a projection (slides 29–33)
Let \(X\) contain the intercept, endogenous regressor(s) and included controls; let \(Z\) contain the intercept, included exogenous controls and excluded instruments. Define the projection matrix
\[
P_Z=Z(Z'Z)^{-1}Z',
\]
assuming \(Z'Z\) is invertible. The first-stage fitted regressors are \(\hat X=P_ZX\). OLS of \(y\) on \(\hat X\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat\beta_{2SLS}
&=(\hat X'\hat X)^{-1}\hat X'y\\
&=(X'P_ZX)^{-1}X'P_Zy,
\end{aligned}
\]
because \(P_Z'=P_Z\) and \(P_Z^2=P_Z\). This is the standard 2SLS estimator. Its existence requires \(X'P_ZX\) to be invertible: the relevant rank condition.
Under the appropriate IV assumptions, this estimator uses instrument-predicted variation to identify the structural coefficients. Inference must account for the IV estimation procedure rather than treating fitted regressors as observed exogenous variables.


8. The Uber application as an IV ratio (slides 35–39)
Write the two equations (suppressing the controls for readability):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log(w_{it})&=\pi_0+\pi_1Z_{it}+X_{it}'\delta+v_{it},\\
\log(h_{it})&=\beta_0+\beta_1\log(w_{it})+X_{it}'\gamma+u_{it}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The lecture reports \(\hat\pi_1=0.20\) and \(\hat\beta_{1,IV}=1.16\). In a just-identified model, the corresponding conditional reduced-form coefficient of the offer on log Uber hours is therefore approximately
\[
\hat\alpha_Z=\hat\beta_{1,IV}\hat\pi_1
\approx1.16\times0.20=0.232.
\]
This 0.232 is an implied calculation, not a separately reported reduced-form estimate in the slides. The IV coefficient is an elasticity, while the first-stage coefficient measures the offer’s effect on log earnings. As in the lecture, inference should account for repeated observations of drivers by clustering standard errors at driver level.

text: Source and scope. Study notes based on Arne Uhlendorff’s Applied Econometrics, Lecture 2 (The Multiple Regression Model; supplied PDF, 50 pages). The explanations and examples are rewritten for learning purposes. The lecture’s five main parts are covered: motivation, OLS mechanics, expected values and omitted-variable bias, sampling variances, and the Gauss–Markov theorem. Mathematical qualifications correct several imprecise statements in the slides. Tutorial exercises and R applications are reserved for later.

title: Class 2
text:
Theory & Intuition

1. Why move from simple to multiple regression?
In simple linear regression, we relate an outcome \(Y\) to one explanatory variable \(X\). But outcomes usually depend on several factors. If an omitted factor affects \(Y\) and is related to \(X\), a simple regression can attribute part of that factor’s association to \(X\).
Multiple regression introduces additional explanatory variables so that we can compare observations holding the included controls fixed. It also allows more flexible functional forms, such as squared terms.
Consider hourly wages:
\[
wage_i=\beta_0+\beta_1 educ_i+\beta_2 exper_i+u_i.
\]
Here, \(educ\) measures years of education and \(exper\) years of labour-market experience. The coefficient \(\beta_1\) describes the change in the modelled wage associated with one more year of education at a given level of experience. Education and experience are allowed to be correlated.






ImportantControlling is not the same as identifying a causal effect



Including experience removes that measured variable from the error term. It does not automatically remove unobserved ability, family background or other confounders. A causal interpretation still requires a credible assumption about the remaining error term.




2. The multiple linear regression model
With \(k\) explanatory variables, the population model is
\[
\boxed{Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_kX_{ik}+u_i.}
\]

\(Y_i\): dependent variable (outcome).
\(X_{ij}\): explanatory variable \(j\) for observation \(i\).
\(\beta_0\): population intercept; \(\beta_j\): population slope coefficients.
\(u_i\): unobserved influences not captured by the included regressors.
\(n\): number of observations; \(k\): number of explanatory variables, excluding the intercept.

The model is linear in its unknown coefficients, not necessarily in the underlying variables. For instance, \(X_1=income\) and \(X_2=income^2\) still produce a linear-in-parameters model.
The central conditional-mean assumption is
\[
\boxed{\mathbb E[u\mid X_1,\ldots,X_k]=0.}
\]
If it holds, the population conditional mean is
\[
\mathbb E[Y\mid X_1,\ldots,X_k]
=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^{k}\beta_jX_j.
\]
This is a strong exogeneity assumption: after conditioning on all included regressors, the remaining unobserved influences have no systematic average relationship with them.


3. Interpreting coefficients: ceteris paribus
For two regressors, the fitted equation is
\[
\widehat Y=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1X_1+\hat\beta_2X_2.
\]
A change in the fitted outcome satisfies
\[
\Delta\widehat Y=\hat\beta_1\Delta X_1+\hat\beta_2\Delta X_2.
\]
If \(X_2\) stays fixed, \(\Delta\widehat Y=\hat\beta_1\Delta X_1\). Thus \(\hat\beta_1\) is a partial slope: it describes the fitted association with \(X_1\) after accounting for \(X_2\). It is not automatically a causal effect.
Example: Suppose a fitted wage equation is
\[
\widehat{wage}=5+0.8\,educ+0.3\,exper.
\]
For two workers with the same experience, one additional year of education corresponds to a fitted wage difference of \(0.8\) wage units. If education rises by one year and experience by two years, the fitted difference is \(0.8+2(0.3)=1.4\) units. These numbers are hypothetical, not estimates from the lecture.


4. Non-linear relationships within linear regression
A quadratic consumption model is
\[
cons=\beta_0+\beta_1inc+\beta_2inc^2+u.
\]
Although the relationship can be curved, OLS remains linear in \(\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2\). Holding \(u\) fixed, the marginal propensity to consume is
\[
\boxed{\frac{\partial cons}{\partial inc}=\beta_1+2\beta_2inc.}
\]
The marginal effect changes with income. It would be meaningless to increase \(inc\) while holding \(inc^2\) fixed: the two regressors are mechanically linked.
The lecture also considers CEO pay:
\[
\log(salary)=\beta_0+\beta_1\log(sales)
+\beta_2ceoten+\beta_3ceoten^2+u.
\]
Here \(\beta_1\) is the elasticity of salary with respect to sales in the specified log relationship, holding other factors fixed. For tenure,
\[
\frac{\partial\log(salary)}{\partial ceoten}
=\beta_2+2\beta_3ceoten.
\]
Multiplying by \(100\) gives the approximate percentage change for one additional year of tenure at a given tenure level. For a finite change \(\Delta t\), the exact change in log salary is \(\beta_2\Delta t+\beta_3[(t+\Delta t)^2-t^2]\); the corresponding percentage change, holding \(u\) fixed, is \(100\{\exp(\Delta\log salary)-1\}\%\).


5. How multiple-regression OLS works
Given observations \(i=1,\ldots,n\), ordinary least squares chooses \(k+1\) coefficients to minimise the sum of squared residuals:
\[
\boxed{\min_{b_0,\ldots,b_k}\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left(Y_i-b_0-\sum_{j=1}^{k}b_jX_{ij}\right)^2.}
\]
After estimation,
\[
\widehat Y_i=\hat\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^{k}\hat\beta_jX_{ij},
\qquad \hat u_i=Y_i-\widehat Y_i.
\]
A residual \(\hat u_i\) is observable once the model has been fitted; the population error \(u_i\) is not. OLS finds the line or hyperplane with the smallest total squared residuals.
Provided the regressors are not perfectly collinear, the OLS solution is unique.


6. Exact sample properties of OLS
With an intercept, the first-order conditions imply
\[
\sum_i\hat u_i=0,
\qquad \sum_iX_{ij}\hat u_i=0\quad(j=1,\ldots,k).
\]
Consequently:

The residuals have sample mean zero.
Every included regressor has zero sample covariance with the residuals.
Fitted values and residuals have zero sample covariance.
\(\overline{\widehat Y}=\bar Y\).
The fitted regression hyperplane passes through \((\bar X_1,\ldots,\bar X_k,\bar Y)\).

These are algebraic properties of the fitted sample, not evidence that the regressors are exogenous in the population.


7. The Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem: partialling out
The Frisch–Waugh–Lovell (FWL) theorem explains what a multiple-regression coefficient measures. To obtain the coefficient on \(X_1\) in a regression of \(Y\) on \(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_k\):

Regress \(X_1\) on an intercept and \(X_2,\ldots,X_k\); retain residuals \(\hat r_{1i}\).
Regress \(Y\) on the same controls; retain residuals \(\hat v_i\).
Regress \(\hat v\) on \(\hat r_1\); its slope equals the coefficient on \(X_1\) in the original multiple regression:

\[
\boxed{\hat\beta_1=
\frac{\sum_i\hat r_{1i}\hat v_i}
{\sum_i\hat r_{1i}^2}.}
\]
Intuition: First remove the variation linearly explained by the controls from both \(X_1\) and \(Y\). Then examine how the remaining variation moves together. This is why we say multiple regression partials out other regressors.
FWL requires the same observations and the same set of controls in the auxiliary regressions, as well as sufficient remaining variation in \(X_1\).


8. The education–IQ example: why coefficients change
The lecture reports a sample of \(759\) workers. Its simple regression is
\[
\widehat{\log(wage)}=1.142+0.099\,educ.
\]
After including an IQ measure, it reports
\[
\widehat{\log(wage)}=1.142+0.073\,educ+0.0076\,IQ.
\]
The estimated schooling coefficient falls from \(0.099\) to \(0.073\): roughly 9.9% to 7.3% using the usual log approximation. The lecture also reports a positive education–IQ correlation of \(0.573\).
Interpretation: The simple regression partly attributes the positive wage association with IQ to education. Controlling for IQ changes the estimated conditional association with schooling. IQ is an imperfect proxy for ability, however, so the multiple-regression coefficient is not automatically a causal return to education.






WarningA transcription issue in the lecture



The slides print the same intercept, \(1.142\), in both wage equations. This is unusual when a regressor is added and could be a slide transcription error. The slope coefficients and the reported correlation are reproduced as shown; the intercepts should not be treated as independently verified without the underlying regression output.




9. Goodness of fit: \(R^2\)
For OLS with an intercept, the lecture uses
\[
\underbrace{\sum_i(Y_i-\bar Y)^2}_{SST}
=\underbrace{\sum_i(\widehat Y_i-\bar Y)^2}_{SSE\;\text{(explained)}}
+\underbrace{\sum_i\hat u_i^2}_{SSR\;\text{(residual)}}.
\]
Thus, when \(SST>0\),
\[
\boxed{R^2=\frac{SSE}{SST}=1-\frac{SSR}{SST}},
\qquad 0\leq R^2\leq1.
\]
Notation warning: The lecture calls the explained sum of squares SSE and the residual sum of squares SSR; other textbooks may use SSE for the error sum of squares. Always check the definitions.
Adding regressors to OLS cannot reduce ordinary \(R^2\) if the outcome and estimation sample stay the same: the old fitted model remains an available option. This does not mean every additional variable improves prediction outside the sample or helps identify causal effects. Adjusted \(R^2\) can fall.


10. Comparing simple and multiple regression
Suppose we estimate, on the same observations,
\[
\widetilde Y=\tilde\beta_0+\tilde\beta_1X_1
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\widehat Y=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1X_1+\hat\beta_2X_2.
\]
Let \(\tilde\delta_1\) be the slope from a simple regression of \(X_2\) on \(X_1\). An exact sample identity is
\[
\boxed{\tilde\beta_1=\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_2\tilde\delta_1.}
\]
The difference between the two estimates depends on (i) the coefficient on the additional variable and (ii) how that variable co-varies with \(X_1\).
With two regressors, the slopes coincide if \(\hat\beta_2=0\) or \(\tilde\delta_1=0\). With several omitted controls, contributions can also cancel; it is not necessary that every omitted coefficient or every correlation be zero.


11. The four assumptions for unbiasedness
The lecture introduces the following assumptions:








Assumption
Statement
Why it matters




MLR.1 — Linear in parameters
\(Y_i=\beta_0+\sum_j\beta_jX_{ij}+u_i\)
Defines the population model


MLR.2 — Random sampling
Observations are independent draws from the population
Connects the sample to the population


MLR.3 — No perfect collinearity
No regressor is an exact linear combination of the intercept and other regressors in the sample
Ensures unique OLS coefficients


MLR.4 — Zero conditional mean
\(E[u_i\mid X_{i1},\ldots,X_{ik}]=0\)
Makes OLS unbiased under the preceding assumptions



Under MLR.1–MLR.4, with the requisite expectations defined,
\[
\boxed{\mathbb E[\hat\beta_j]=\beta_j,\qquad j=0,\ldots,k.}
\]
Unbiased means the estimator’s expectation across repeated samples equals the true coefficient; it does not mean each sample estimate is close to the truth.


12. Perfect collinearity versus high correlation
Perfect collinearity occurs when one included regressor is an exact linear combination of the intercept and the others. OLS then cannot determine all coefficients uniquely.
Two examples from the lecture:

Logarithms: For positive income, \(\log(inc^2)=2\log(inc)\). Including both as separate regressors is redundant. By contrast, \([\log(inc)]^2\) is generally not equal to \(\log(inc^2)\).
Election spending: If \(totalspend=spend_A+spend_B\), including all three with an intercept creates an exact linear dependence. One must remove or reparameterise a variable.

High but imperfect correlation is permitted. It can make coefficients imprecise, but does not by itself make OLS undefined or biased.
The rank condition requires at least \(n\geq k+1\) observations for a unique fit; estimating the error variance using residual degrees of freedom additionally requires \(n>k+1\).


13. Omitted-variable bias (OVB)
Suppose the correct population model is
\[
Y=\beta_0+\beta_1X_1+\beta_2X_2+u,
\qquad E[u\mid X_1,X_2]=0.
\]
If we omit \(X_2\) and regress \(Y\) on \(X_1\) alone, the omitted term \(\beta_2X_2+u\) becomes the error. The resulting slope generally does not estimate \(\beta_1\) without bias.
Let
\[
\delta_1=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_2)}
{\operatorname{Var}(X_1)},
\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X_1)>0.
\]
The population simple-regression slope is
\[
\boxed{\beta_1^{simple}=\beta_1+\beta_2\delta_1.}
\]
Hence the difference between the population simple slope and the desired partial slope is \(\beta_2\delta_1\). This is the familiar OVB formula at the population linear-projection level.

Wage example: If ability raises wages and is positively associated with education, omitting ability tends to push the simple schooling slope upwards relative to the coefficient that controls for ability.






ImportantDo not confuse a sample identity with an expected bias



The exact identity \(\tilde\beta_1=\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_2\tilde\delta_1\) uses sample estimates. Because \(\tilde\delta_1\) is random, it is generally incorrect to write \(E[\hat\beta_2\tilde\delta_1]=E[\hat\beta_2]\tilde\delta_1\) without conditioning. Under the full-model assumptions, the correct conditional statement is
\[
E[\tilde\beta_1\mid\mathbf X]=\beta_1+\beta_2\tilde\delta_1,
\]
where \(\mathbf X\) contains both regressors for all observations. Unconditionally, the bias is \(\beta_2E[\tilde\delta_1]\), when that expectation exists. The population formula above uses the non-random population projection slope \(\delta_1\).




14. Adding irrelevant variables
An irrelevant variable has a true partial coefficient of zero. If the full model still satisfies MLR.1–MLR.4, including it does not introduce bias into the OLS coefficients.
However, extra regressors consume degrees of freedom and may increase estimator variance. The practical distinction is:

Omitting a relevant confounder can introduce bias.
Including an irrelevant regressor need not introduce bias, but can reduce precision.

These are not unconditional rules: they depend on the maintained model assumptions.


15. Homoskedasticity and heteroskedasticity
To study the sampling variance of OLS, the lecture adds:
\[
\boxed{\text{MLR.5: }\operatorname{Var}(u\mid X_1,\ldots,X_k)=\sigma^2.}
\]
This is homoskedasticity: the conditional error variance is constant across regressor values. Heteroskedasticity means that conditional variance changes with the regressors.
Example: Wage outcomes may be more dispersed among highly educated workers than among workers with fewer years of education. That would be consistent with heteroskedasticity even if the conditional mean were correctly specified.
MLR.5 is not needed for unbiasedness under MLR.1–MLR.4. It is needed for the simple conventional OLS variance formula and the standard Gauss–Markov efficiency result. With heteroskedasticity, heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors can be appropriate under further regularity conditions; they do not repair endogeneity.


16. What determines the precision of OLS?
For regressor \(X_j\), define
\[
SST_j=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_{ij}-\bar X_j)^2.
\]
Let \(R_j^2\) be the \(R^2\) from regressing \(X_j\) on an intercept and all the other regressors. Under MLR.1–MLR.5,
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_j\mid\mathbf X)
=\frac{\sigma^2}{SST_j(1-R_j^2)},\quad j=1,\ldots,k.}
\]
Three forces determine precision, holding the others fixed:

Noise: Larger error variance \(\sigma^2\) means less precise estimates.
Variation: Larger \(SST_j\) means more information about the slope.
Multicollinearity: Larger \(R_j^2\) means that less of \(X_j\) is distinct from the other regressors, increasing variance.

When \(R_j^2\to1\) with \(SST_j\) and \(\sigma^2\) fixed, the conditional variance grows without bound. At \(R_j^2=1\), the coefficient is not separately identified by OLS.






NoteDoes adding a control improve precision?



Not necessarily. A useful control may reduce the population residual variance of the newly specified model, but it may also increase \(R_j^2\) and reduce residual degrees of freedom. Adding regressors therefore has an ambiguous effect on the precision of an existing slope. It cannot increase the sample residual sum of squares when the estimation sample is unchanged, but that is a different statement.




17. Estimating the error variance and standard errors
Because \(u_i\) is unobserved, we estimate its variance using residuals. Under MLR.1–MLR.5 and \(n>k+1\),
\[
\boxed{\hat\sigma^2=
\frac{\sum_i\hat u_i^2}{n-k-1}
=\frac{SSR}{n-k-1}.}
\]
The denominator is the residual degrees of freedom: \(n\) observations minus \(k+1\) fitted coefficients. Under the assumptions, \(E[\hat\sigma^2]=\sigma^2\).
The estimated standard deviation of the regression error is \(\hat\sigma=\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2}\). The conventional homoskedastic standard error of a slope is
\[
\boxed{se(\hat\beta_j)=
\frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{SST_j(1-R_j^2)}}.}
\]
A standard error measures the estimated sampling uncertainty of a coefficient, not the size of the residual for an individual observation. The square root \(\hat\sigma\) is not generally an unbiased estimator of \(\sigma\), even though \(\hat\sigma^2\) is unbiased for \(\sigma^2\).
Under suitable large-sample conditions, slope standard errors often shrink at approximately \(1/\sqrt n\). This rate is not automatic if regressor variation or collinearity deteriorates as \(n\) increases.


18. The Gauss–Markov theorem: why OLS?
Under MLR.1–MLR.5, OLS is BLUE:

Best Linear Unbiased Estimator: Among estimators that are linear in the observed outcomes and unbiased for the regression coefficients, OLS has the smallest conditional variance (or, jointly, a covariance matrix no larger in the positive-semidefinite sense).

“Linear” means linear in the observed \(Y_i\) values, with weights that may depend on the regressors. “Best” means minimum variance within this restricted class, not best under every possible criterion.
The theorem does not establish that OLS is causal, normally distributed, unbiased under endogeneity, or more efficient than every conceivable non-linear or biased estimator. It also does not justify conventional homoskedastic standard errors when MLR.5 fails.






ImportantWhat to remember from Class 2



Multiple regression estimates partial associations. For a causal interpretation, the main obstacle remains exogeneity: \(E[u\mid X_1,\ldots,X_k]=0\). MLR.1–MLR.4 give unbiasedness; adding MLR.5 gives the conventional variance formula and the Gauss–Markov BLUE result. More controls do not automatically mean less bias or more precision.

title: Class 2
text:
Mathematical Derivations

1. The conditional mean and partial slopes
Start from
\[
Y=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^{k}\beta_jX_j+u.
\]
Under \(E[u\mid X_1,\ldots,X_k]=0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
E[Y\mid X_1,\ldots,X_k]
&=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^{k}\beta_jX_j
+E[u\mid X_1,\ldots,X_k]\\
&=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^{k}\beta_jX_j.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, holding all other regressors fixed,
\[
\boxed{\frac{\partial E[Y\mid X_1,\ldots,X_k]}
{\partial X_j}=\beta_j.}
\]
This is a derivative of the conditional mean. Its causal interpretation requires the additional substantive conditions needed to interpret changes in \(X_j\) as interventions.


2. Deriving the OLS normal equations
Define the objective
\[
Q(b_0,\ldots,b_k)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left(Y_i-b_0-\sum_{j=1}^{k}b_jX_{ij}\right)^2.
\]
Step 1 — Differentiate with respect to the intercept:
\[
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial b_0}
=-2\sum_i\left(Y_i-b_0-\sum_jb_jX_{ij}\right)=0.
\]
At the minimum,
\[
\boxed{\sum_i\hat u_i=0.}
\]
Step 2 — Differentiate with respect to each slope \(b_j\):
\[
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial b_j}
=-2\sum_iX_{ij}\left(Y_i-b_0-\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}b_\ell X_{i\ell}\right)=0.
\]
Hence,
\[
\boxed{\sum_iX_{ij}\hat u_i=0,\qquad j=1,\ldots,k.}
\]
These \(k+1\) equations are the normal equations. They are also sample analogues of the population moment conditions \(E[u]=0\) and \(E[X_ju]=0\). The latter follow from zero conditional mean (when the relevant expectations exist), but are weaker than it.


3. Matrix formula for multiple-regression OLS
This is a compact extension of the lecture’s normal equations. Let \(\mathbf y\) be the \(n\times1\) outcome vector, \(\mathbf X\) the \(n\times(k+1)\) design matrix including a column of ones, and \(\boldsymbol\beta\) the coefficient vector. Then
\[
\mathbf y=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta+\mathbf u.
\]
OLS minimises
\[
Q(\mathbf b)=(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\mathbf b)'(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\mathbf b).
\]
Expanding and differentiating,
\[
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial\mathbf b}
=-2\mathbf X'\mathbf y+2\mathbf X'\mathbf X\mathbf b=\mathbf0.
\]
If \(\mathbf X\) has full column rank, \(\mathbf X'\mathbf X\) is invertible and
\[
\boxed{\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X'\mathbf y.}
\]
Because the objective is a convex quadratic and the design has full column rank, this solution is the unique global minimum.


4. Deriving the residual properties
The normal equations give \(\mathbf X'\hat{\mathbf u}=\mathbf0\). Since the intercept column is part of \(\mathbf X\),
\[
\sum_i\hat u_i=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bar Y=\overline{\widehat Y}.
\]
Because \(\widehat{\mathbf y}=\mathbf X\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\),
\[
\widehat{\mathbf y}'\hat{\mathbf u}
=\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}'\mathbf X'\hat{\mathbf u}=0.
\]
Finally, taking sample averages of the fitted equation yields
\[
\boxed{\bar Y=\hat\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^{k}\hat\beta_j\bar X_j.}
\]
Thus the fitted hyperplane passes through the vector of sample means.


5. Proving the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem
Write the design matrix as \(\mathbf X=[\mathbf x_1\;\mathbf Z]\), where \(\mathbf Z\) contains the intercept and all controls other than \(\mathbf x_1\). Assume \(\mathbf Z\) has full column rank and \(\mathbf x_1\) is not in its column space.
Define the residual-maker matrix
\[
\mathbf M_Z=\mathbf I-\mathbf Z(\mathbf Z'\mathbf Z)^{-1}\mathbf Z'.
\]
It removes the component linearly explained by \(\mathbf Z\):
\[
\hat{\mathbf r}_1=\mathbf M_Z\mathbf x_1,
\qquad \hat{\mathbf v}=\mathbf M_Z\mathbf y.
\]
The full regression is \(\mathbf y=\mathbf x_1\hat\beta_1+\mathbf Z\hat{\boldsymbol\gamma}+\hat{\mathbf u}\). Multiplying by \(\mathbf M_Z\) eliminates the controls because \(\mathbf M_Z\mathbf Z=0\):
\[
\mathbf M_Z\mathbf y
=\mathbf M_Z\mathbf x_1\hat\beta_1+\mathbf M_Z\hat{\mathbf u}.
\]
The full-model normal equations imply \(\mathbf x_1'\hat{\mathbf u}=0\) and \(\mathbf Z'\hat{\mathbf u}=0\), so \(\mathbf M_Z\hat{\mathbf u}=\hat{\mathbf u}\). Premultiplying by \(\hat{\mathbf r}_1'\) therefore gives
\[
\hat{\mathbf r}_1'\hat{\mathbf v}
=\hat\beta_1\hat{\mathbf r}_1'\hat{\mathbf r}_1.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{\hat\beta_1
=\frac{\hat{\mathbf r}_1'\hat{\mathbf v}}
{\hat{\mathbf r}_1'\hat{\mathbf r}_1}
=\frac{\sum_i\hat r_{1i}\hat v_i}
{\sum_i\hat r_{1i}^2}.}
\]
The residuals from both auxiliary regressions have mean zero because \(\mathbf Z\) contains an intercept, so the final regression’s intercept is zero.


6. Deriving the \(R^2\) decomposition
For every observation,
\[
Y_i-\bar Y=(\widehat Y_i-\bar Y)+\hat u_i.
\]
Square and sum:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_i(Y_i-\bar Y)^2
&=\sum_i(\widehat Y_i-\bar Y)^2+\sum_i\hat u_i^2\\
&\quad+2\sum_i(\widehat Y_i-\bar Y)\hat u_i.
\end{aligned}
\]
The cross-term is zero because \(\sum_i\widehat Y_i\hat u_i=0\) and \(\sum_i\hat u_i=0\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{SST=SSE+SSR},\qquad
\boxed{R^2=1-\frac{SSR}{SST}}.
\]
Adding a regressor enlarges the set of candidate fitted models. The minimum attainable \(SSR\) therefore cannot increase on an unchanged dataset; consequently ordinary \(R^2\) cannot fall.


7. Deriving the exact simple-versus-multiple regression identity
The fitted multiple regression gives the sample identity
\[
Y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1X_{i1}
+\hat\beta_2X_{i2}+\hat u_i.
\]
The simple-regression slope is
\[
\tilde\beta_1=
\frac{\sum_i(X_{i1}-\bar X_1)(Y_i-\bar Y)}
{\sum_i(X_{i1}-\bar X_1)^2}.
\]
Substitute the fitted multiple-regression equation. The intercept term disappears after demeaning, and the residual term disappears because OLS makes \(X_1\) orthogonal to \(\hat u\):
\[
\tilde\beta_1=\hat\beta_1
+\hat\beta_2\frac{\sum_i(X_{i1}-\bar X_1)(X_{i2}-\bar X_2)}
{\sum_i(X_{i1}-\bar X_1)^2}.
\]
The final ratio is precisely the slope \(\tilde\delta_1\) from regressing \(X_2\) on \(X_1\). Thus
\[
\boxed{\tilde\beta_1=\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_2\tilde\delta_1.}
\]
With several additional regressors, the corresponding identity is
\[
\tilde\beta_1=\hat\beta_1+\sum_{j=2}^{k}\hat\beta_j\tilde\delta_j,
\]
where \(\tilde\delta_j\) is the simple-regression slope of \(X_j\) on \(X_1\). The sum can equal zero through cancellation even when individual terms are non-zero.


8. Deriving omitted-variable bias correctly
Assume the true model is
\[
Y=\beta_0+\beta_1X_1+\beta_2X_2+u,
\qquad E[u\mid X_1,X_2]=0.
\]
Population derivation. The slope in the population linear projection of \(Y\) on an intercept and \(X_1\) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\beta_1^{simple}
&=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(X_1)}\\
&=\frac{\beta_1\operatorname{Var}(X_1)
+\beta_2\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_2)
+\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,u)}{\operatorname{Var}(X_1)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Zero conditional mean implies \(\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,u)=0\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{\beta_1^{simple}-\beta_1
=\beta_2\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_2)}
{\operatorname{Var}(X_1)}=\beta_2\delta_1.}
\]
Finite-sample conditional derivation. Let \(\tilde\delta_1\) be the sample slope from regressing \(X_2\) on \(X_1\). Direct substitution into the simple OLS formula gives
\[
\tilde\beta_1
=\beta_1+\beta_2\tilde\delta_1
+\frac{\sum_i(X_{i1}-\bar X_1)u_i}{\sum_i(X_{i1}-\bar X_1)^2}.
\]
Under random sampling and zero conditional mean, conditioning on the full observed regressor matrix \(\mathbf X\) yields
\[
\boxed{E[\tilde\beta_1\mid\mathbf X]
=\beta_1+\beta_2\tilde\delta_1.}
\]
This is the conditional bias, given the realised regressors. The unconditional finite-sample bias is \(\beta_2E[\tilde\delta_1]\), provided that expectation exists. Do not treat the random \(\tilde\delta_1\) as a constant inside an unconditional expectation.


9. Proving unbiasedness of multiple-regression OLS
Start with the population model in matrix form:
\[
\mathbf y=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta+\mathbf u.
\]
Substitute into the OLS formula:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
&=(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X'(\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta+\mathbf u)\\
&=\boldsymbol\beta+(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X'\mathbf u.
\end{aligned}
\]
Under MLR.2 and MLR.4, \(E[\mathbf u\mid\mathbf X]=\mathbf0\). Therefore, conditional on a full-rank \(\mathbf X\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
E[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\mid\mathbf X]
&=\boldsymbol\beta+(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X'E[\mathbf u\mid\mathbf X]\\
&=\boxed{\boldsymbol\beta}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking expectations again gives
\[
\boxed{E[\hat\beta_j]=\beta_j,\qquad j=0,\ldots,k.}
\]
This proof uses MLR.1–MLR.4. Homoskedasticity is not required.


10. Deriving the conditional variance of OLS
From the previous identity,
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\boldsymbol\beta
=(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X'\mathbf u.
\]
Under independent random sampling and MLR.5, the conditional error covariance matrix is \(\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf u\mid\mathbf X)=\sigma^2\mathbf I\). Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\mid\mathbf X)
&=(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X'
(\sigma^2\mathbf I)\mathbf X(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\\
&=\boxed{\sigma^2(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
To obtain the variance of slope \(j\), use FWL. Let \(\hat r_{ji}\) be residuals from regressing \(X_j\) on an intercept and all other regressors. Then
\[
\hat\beta_j-\beta_j
=\frac{\sum_i\hat r_{ji}u_i}{\sum_i\hat r_{ji}^2}.
\]
Conditioning on \(\mathbf X\),
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_j\mid\mathbf X)
=\frac{\sigma^2\sum_i\hat r_{ji}^2}
{\left(\sum_i\hat r_{ji}^2\right)^2}
=\frac{\sigma^2}{\sum_i\hat r_{ji}^2}.
\]
From the auxiliary regression’s \(R_j^2\) definition,
\[
\sum_i\hat r_{ji}^2=SST_j(1-R_j^2).
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_j\mid\mathbf X)
=\frac{\sigma^2}{SST_j(1-R_j^2)}.}
\]
This derivation makes the multicollinearity penalty explicit: the relevant information is the part of \(X_j\) that cannot be linearly predicted by the other regressors.


11. Why divide by \(n-k-1\) to estimate \(\sigma^2\)?
Let \(\mathbf H=\mathbf X(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X'\) be the projection matrix and \(\mathbf M=\mathbf I-\mathbf H\) the residual-maker matrix. Then
\[
\hat{\mathbf u}=\mathbf M\mathbf y=\mathbf M\mathbf u,
\]
because \(\mathbf M\mathbf X=0\). The residual sum of squares is
\[
SSR=\hat{\mathbf u}'\hat{\mathbf u}=\mathbf u'\mathbf M\mathbf u.
\]
Conditional on \(\mathbf X\), use \(E[\mathbf u\mid\mathbf X]=\mathbf0\) and \(E[\mathbf u\mathbf u'\mid\mathbf X]=\sigma^2\mathbf I\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
E[SSR\mid\mathbf X]
&=E[\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf M\mathbf u\mathbf u')\mid\mathbf X]\\
&=\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf M\sigma^2\mathbf I)\\
&=\sigma^2\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf M).
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(\mathbf H\) projects onto a \((k+1)\)-dimensional column space,
\[
\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf M)=n-(k+1)=n-k-1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{E\left[\frac{SSR}{n-k-1}\middle|\mathbf X\right]
=\sigma^2.}
\]
Dividing by \(n\) instead would give conditional expectation \(\sigma^2(n-k-1)/n\) and bias \(-\sigma^2(k+1)/n\).


12. Proving the Gauss–Markov theorem (BLUE)
Consider any other estimator \(\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta}=\mathbf A\mathbf y\) that is linear in \(\mathbf y\) and conditionally unbiased for every possible \(\boldsymbol\beta\). Conditional unbiasedness requires
\[
\mathbf A\mathbf X=\mathbf I.
\]
Define the OLS weight matrix
\[
\mathbf A_0=(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X',
\]
and write \(\mathbf A=\mathbf A_0+\mathbf D\). Since both estimators are unbiased, \(\mathbf D\mathbf X=\mathbf0\).
Under homoskedasticity,
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta}\mid\mathbf X)
=\sigma^2(\mathbf A_0+\mathbf D)(\mathbf A_0+\mathbf D)'.
\]
The cross-terms vanish because
\[
\mathbf A_0\mathbf D'
=(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X'\mathbf D'=\mathbf0.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta}\mid\mathbf X)
-\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\mid\mathbf X)
=\sigma^2\mathbf D\mathbf D'.}
\]
For any vector \(\mathbf a\),
\[
\mathbf a'(\sigma^2\mathbf D\mathbf D')\mathbf a
=\sigma^2\|\mathbf D'\mathbf a\|^2\geq0.
\]
Therefore the difference is positive semidefinite: no other linear conditionally unbiased estimator has a smaller conditional variance for any coefficient or linear combination of coefficients. This is the Gauss–Markov result.






NoteLimits of these proofs



The proofs establish OLS algebra, unbiasedness under MLR.1–MLR.4, and conventional variance/BLUE results under MLR.1–MLR.5. They do not establish that the assumptions hold for a given dataset. In particular, good fit, zero sample residual correlations and small standard errors do not prove a causal interpretation. Normality is not one of the five Gauss–Markov assumptions; exact small-sample \(t\) inference requires further conditions.
